title: Technology and local suitability

blocks.heading: Technology and local suitability
blocks.text: Technology applies knowledge, tools and processes to practical tasks; simple, intermediate and complex describe broad levels of sophistication. Appropriate technology is judged by fit to purpose and local conditions, so it may be simple, intermediate or complex. Ask what output is required and what skills, materials, power, finance and repair arrangements are available. The most sophisticated machine may be unsuitable if a missing spare part stops it for months. A less complex tool may be unsuitable where it cannot meet the required safety or output standard.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Simple technology
blocks.text: Simple technology uses relatively straightforward tools or processes requiring limited technical complexity. A simple tool may be easy to operate or repair locally, but its capacity and labour requirements may limit its suitability. A hand hoe is an example. Calling it simple does not establish that it is the best tool for every farming task. Compare it with the area, available time and users’ capabilities rather than treating simple as a synonym for appropriate.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Intermediate technology
blocks.text: Intermediate technology is technology between very simple and highly complex forms, often designed to use accessible skills and resources. Whether it is appropriate depends on the local purpose and conditions. An intermediate device may increase productive capacity without requiring the infrastructure or specialist maintenance of a highly complex system. A locally repairable pedal-powered device can illustrate the idea where it meets the task. The category is relative, not a fixed technical specification. An example should state what it does and why its level of complexity fits the setting.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Complex technology
blocks.text: Complex technology uses comparatively sophisticated equipment, processes or control systems and generally needs more specialised support. It can provide precision or high capacity, but may depend on skilled operators, power, maintenance and available parts. A computer-controlled cutting machine illustrates sophisticated control. Its potential precision is useful only if the workshop can install, operate and maintain it. High purchase cost alone is not a complete definition of complexity.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Appropriate technology
blocks.text: Appropriate technology is technology suited to the local purpose, resources, skills, costs and environmental conditions; it need not be the most complex option. Suitability can change with the task and available support; a technology is not appropriate simply because it is simple or locally made. An invented workshop without reliable electricity might choose a usable manual tool for a modest order. A large precision order with reliable power and trained staff may justify a more complex option. In both cases the judgement concerns fit, not a permanent ranking of machines.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Appropriateness can change
blocks.text: An invented workshop makes small repair batches and has skilled hand workers, manual tools and no reliable electricity. Repairable manual equipment may fit better than an electrically dependent automated line. A different workshop with large standardised orders, trained technicians and reliable power may reasonably choose the line. Neither case says simple technology is always better. The decisive evidence is the relationship between the task, support and productive capacity.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Connect production to development
blocks.text: Energy supply and labour skills affect technological suitability. Connect the tool to its users and task; an appropriate choice may belong to any level of complexity.
